source_text: Ostendit Apostolus non a se dictum esse, peccatum generatione transisse, quando nominans hominem, adiecit: unum; unus enim numeri principium est; et ille explicans per quem diceret intrasse peccatum, non solum eum nominavit, verum etiam numeravit: Per unum, inquit, hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit [n70] . Hic autem unus praebendae imitationi sufficit, generationi implendae non sufficit. Peccatum autem transiit, sed per unum. Manifestum est, imitationem hic, non generationem coargui, quae nisi per duos fieri non potest. Aut igitur ostende, per Adam solum sine muliere generationem exstitisse; nec hoc enim ab elegantia tui abhorret ingenii; aut certe quoniam vides generationem nisi per duos constare non posse, assentire vel sero, accusatum non esse per unum numerum opus duorum. Per unum, inquit, hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, qui dixit: per unum, intellegi per duos noluit. Quid rogo, quaerebat inter haec dogmata numerus, ut Apostolus tanta cura, non solum hominem, sed unum hominem nominaret? Verum apparet cautus augusti sermo consilii, qui revelante Spiritu Sancto, temporum nostrorum praecavit et exarmavit errores; ne in infamationem quippe aliquid instituti a Deo coniugii vel benedictae fecunditatis dixisse putaretur; cum causa posceret ut peccati replicaret exordia, per eum dixit numerum transisse peccatum, qui fetibus non poterat convenire. Et certe primi homines ambo deliquerant, qui ambo merito vocantur forma posteris fuisse peccati; cur non igitur Apostolus per duos ait transisse peccatum; quod et ad fidem magis historiae congruebat? Verum nihil potuit ab eo prudentius fieri; vidit enim, si duos nominasset, qui praevaricationi initium exemplumque praestiterant, et per eos affirmasset transisse peccatum, errori occasionem patere, ut putaretur per duorum nomina coniunctionem fecunditatemque damnasse. Ideoque prudentissime unum maluit nominare, qui non sufficiens ad generationis indicium, ad signum abundaret exempli; atque imitationem accusatus gravaret, nec fecunditatem numeratus argueret. Et ut breviter quod egimus colligatur, fecunditas in primis hominibus instituta, nisi per duos agi non potest; peccatum autem Apostolus intrasse pronuntiat, sed per unum.
pass_a_gloss: The Apostle showed that it was not said by him that sin passed by generation, when, naming a human being, he added: one; for one is the beginning of number; and he, unfolding through whom he said sin had entered, not only named him but also numbered him: Through one, he says, human being sin entered into this world. But this one suffices for furnishing imitation, it does not suffice for filling generation. But sin passed, but through one. It is manifest that imitation is here convicted, not generation, which cannot be done except through two. Either therefore show that through Adam alone without a woman generation existed; for not even this shudders away from the elegance of your talent; or certainly, since you see that generation cannot stand except through two, assent even late that the work of two has not been accused through the number one. Through one, he says, human being sin entered into the world, who said: through one, did not want it to be understood through two. What, I ask, was number seeking among these dogmas, that the Apostle with so great care named not only a human being but one human being? But there appears a cautious speech of lofty counsel, which, with the Holy Spirit revealing, forestalled and disarmed the errors of our times; lest namely he be thought to have said anything toward a slander of a conjunction instituted by God or of blessed fecundity; when the cause demanded that he unfold the beginnings of sin, he said that sin passed through that number which could not fit offspring. And certainly the first human beings had both offended, who both are meritedly called to have been a form of sin for posterity; why therefore did the Apostle not say that sin passed through two; which also agreed more with the faith of the history? But nothing could have been done by him more prudently; for he saw that if he had named two, who had furnished the beginning and example of transgression, and had affirmed that sin passed through them, an occasion of error would lie open, that he be thought through the names of two to have damned conjunction and fecundity. And therefore most prudently he preferred to name one, who, not sufficing toward an indication of generation, would abound toward a sign of example; and, accused, would load imitation, nor, numbered, would accuse fecundity. And that what we have done may be collected briefly, fecundity instituted in the first human beings cannot be acted except through two; but the Apostle pronounces that sin entered, but through one.

pass_b_english: The apostle showed that he was not saying sin passed on by generation when, naming a human being, he added ‘one.’ One is the beginning of number. Explaining through whom he said sin had entered, he not only named him but also counted him: ‘Through one man sin entered this world’ (Romans 5:12). This one person is sufficient to supply an example for imitation but insufficient to accomplish generation. Sin passed on, but through one. Clearly, then, what is accused here is imitation, not generation, which cannot take place except through two. Either show that generation occurred through Adam alone, without a woman—that would hardly be inconsistent with the refinement of your mind—or else, since you see that generation cannot exist without two, agree at last that the work of two was not accused by the number one. ‘Through one man,’ he says, ‘sin entered the world.’ In saying ‘through one,’ he did not mean us to understand ‘through two.’ Why, I ask, was number brought into these teachings, so that the apostle took such care to name not merely a human being but one human being? We see here the careful language of a lofty purpose: through the Holy Spirit’s revelation it anticipated and disarmed the errors of our times. When the subject required him to recount sin’s beginnings, he said sin passed on through a number that could not fit procreation, so that no one would think he had said anything to slander marriage instituted by God or blessed fertility. Certainly the first two human beings had both sinned, and both can rightly be called models of sin for their descendants. Why, then, did the apostle not say that sin passed on through two, which would have agreed better with the historical account? Nothing could have been wiser than his action. He saw that if he named the two who had provided the beginning and example of transgression, and affirmed that sin passed through them, there would be an opening for error: someone might think that by naming two he had condemned their union and fertility. Very wisely, therefore, he preferred to name one. Insufficient to indicate generation, one was more than enough to signify an example: accusing him would condemn imitation, while counting him would not accuse fertility. To sum up our argument briefly: the fertility instituted in the first human beings cannot operate except through two; but the apostle declares that sin entered through one.

choices.why: Julian's Rom 5:12 reading: sin passes by copying Adam's example, not by generation/seed.
Julian's target is Augustine's claim that sin is transmitted by begetting; keep generation vs imitation.
